title: How Long You Really Last
description: Your water budget, what dehydration does, and why the rule of threes misleads
tryIt: On a warm day, note the colour of your pee each time you go, and see how it changes when you sip a glass of water every hour.

concepts.title: How it works: the water budget
concepts.contentHtml:
It is two in the afternoon, the car will not start, the road is empty in both directions and you have half a litre of warm water. The question that matters now is not how long until help comes, but how fast your body is spending the water it already has.

You are mostly water: a review in Nutrition Reviews puts it at about 75% of body weight in infants and 55% in the elderly, and states bluntly that without water, humans can survive only for days.1 You lose water all the time by sweating, urinating and defecating. The US Army's survival manual reckons that at 20 °C the average adult doing ordinary work loses, and so needs, 2 to 3 litres a day.2 Some comes back in food (about 22% of Americans' water, by one estimate); the rest you must drink.

Your kidneys keep the accounts. When you run short, a hormone called vasopressin tells them to make a smaller volume of more concentrated urine, which is why pee turns dark. They cannot shut down altogether, though: the Army's rule is to drink enough to keep producing at least half a litre of urine every 24 hours. Sweat is the big, uncontrolled spend. Water lost through the skin ranges from about 0.3 litres an hour sitting still to 2 litres an hour working hard in the heat.3

The Army learned this the hard way. Preparing to fight in North Africa in the Second World War, it tried to train soldiers to need less water by cutting their supply step by step, a scheme it called water discipline. It caused hundreds of heat casualties.4 The body simply needs what the heat and the work demand, and hard work in the sun at 43 °C takes 19 litres a day.5

concepts.title: In the field: the first hour
concepts.contentHtml:
You cannot make water appear in the first hour, but you can stop wasting it. The Army's desert advice rests on one idea: conserve your sweat, not your water. Water inside you keeps you cool and thinking clearly; water saved in a bottle while you collapse from heat does nothing.

  1. Get out of the sun. Find or rig shade, and put something between you and the hot ground. In the shade the air can be 11 to 17 °C cooler.1
  2. Stop moving. Rest through the heat of the day and save any work for the cool of the evening and night.
  3. Keep your clothes on. Sleeves down, head covered, a scarf round your neck: clothing holds sweat against your skin so you get its full cooling effect.
  4. Shut your mouth. Staying quietly in the shade, not talking, breathing through your nose, makes your water need drop dramatically.2
  5. Sip on a schedule. Most people cannot comfortably drink more than a litre at a time,3 so drink small amounts at regular intervals even when you are not thirsty.
  6. If water is short, do not eat. Digesting food uses water you need for cooling.4
  7. Watch your pee. A light colour means you are drinking enough; dark means drink more.
Safety If you have a signal, call the emergency services first. The NHS lists thirst, headache, dark strong-smelling pee, dizziness, tiredness and a dry mouth as signs of dehydration, and says to call 999 (in the UK) if someone with those signs also has cold, pale or blotchy skin, fast breathing or confusion, which can mean shock.5 Someone who stops sweating while working hard in the heat may be developing heat stroke, a medical emergency.

concepts.title: Myth check: the rule of threes
concepts.contentHtml:
Every survival book seems to quote the same neat formula. Oregon State University's preparedness guide lists it like this: you can live 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter, 3 days without water1 and 3 weeks without food.

Myth You have three days without water, so there is no hurry.
Reality There is no fixed clock. The rule is a fair order of priorities, not a timetable. Your water budget depends on heat and work: 2 to 3 litres a day at 20 °C, 19 litres for hard work in the sun at 43 °C, and in an extreme, dry climate a person can lose 2.5 to 3.5 litres an hour.2 The Army warns that you cannot survive long without water in high desert temperatures.3 Water is, as one review puts it, a nutrient whose absence will be lethal within days;4 how many days depends on you and your surroundings.
Myth Your body will tell you when to drink.
Reality Thirst is a late alarm. The Army manual lists it last among the signs of dehydration, because you are already about 2 percent dehydrated by the time you crave fluids,5 and a person who drinks only when thirsty takes in about two-thirds of what they need.6

Wait, really? The Army changed its own advice. Its 1992 manual told survivors to ration water sensibly until they found a source.7 The 2002 edition rewrote the line: ration your sweat, not your water.8 Its desert chapter is blunter still: do not ration your water, because if you try you stand a good chance of becoming a heat casualty.9

title: Finding Water
description: Reading the land, catching rain and dew, plants that hold water, and why a solar still disappoints
tryIt: On a dewy morning, in a garden or field where you are allowed, tie an old cotton T-shirt round your ankles, walk through long grass before breakfast and wring it into a jug to see how much dew you collect.

concepts.title: How it works: reading the land
concepts.contentHtml:
Day two. The bottle is empty, your lips are cracking and the land looks bone dry. It almost never is. The Army's manual opens its water chapter by saying that almost any environment has water present to some degree.1 Your job is to think like water, which runs downhill, gathers in low places and hides under the surface long after the top has dried.

So look low. The manual's list of places to dig is a lesson in how water moves: valleys and low areas, the foot of the concave bank on the outside of a bend in a dry river, the foot of cliffs and rock outcrops, the first hollow behind the first sand dune of a dry lake, and anywhere you find damp surface sand or green plants. Dig a hole deep enough to let water seep in, then wait.2

Then read the living things, because they need water too. Grazing animals such as deer are rarely far from it and drink at dawn and dusk,3 and game trails that converge often lead to it. Grain-eating birds such as finches and pigeons are never far from water: when they fly straight and low they are heading for it,4 and on the way back, full, they hop from tree to tree. Bees or ants going into a hole in a tree may point to water inside, and in dry country bird droppings around a crack in the rock can mean water in or near the crack.5

Not every clue is honest. Meat-eaters get their moisture from what they eat and can go a long time without drinking; water birds fly long distances without stopping; birds of prey get their liquid from their victims. None of them is a reliable guide.6

concepts.title: In the field: rain, dew and plants
concepts.contentHtml:
The easiest water to make safe is water that never touched the ground. Rain and dew come out of the sky nearly clean, and a few plants store water you can tap.

  1. Catch the rain. Spread a tarp, poncho or plastic sheet with a low point over a container. Let the first rush of a shower run off: health agencies recommend a "first flush" diverter on roofs because that first water picks up the most dirt and germs.1
  2. Mop the dew. Before sunrise, tie rags or tufts of fine grass round your ankles, walk through the wet grass, then wring them into a container. Aboriginal Australians, the manual notes, sometimes mop up as much as a litre an hour this way.2
  3. Wipe the cold metal. In deserts the big swing between night and day temperatures can leave condensation on metal surfaces; soak it up with a cloth and wring it out.
  4. Tap the bamboo. Green bamboo is an excellent source.3 Bend a green stalk over, tie it down and cut off the top, and water drips out through the night.
  5. Bag a branch. Tie a clear plastic bag over a leafy branch so the plant's own moisture collects inside. The same limb can be used for 3 to 5 days without lasting harm.4
  6. Treat it anyway. The manual counts rain caught in clean containers as usually safe, but the US CDC warns that rainwater is not necessarily safe to drink without first removing germs and chemicals.5 When in doubt, boil.
Safety Only cut or bag plants where you are allowed to, and never use a plant you cannot identify for certain: the manual warns that poisonous vegetation gives poisonous liquid. It also warns that plant sap kept longer than 24 hours starts to ferment and becomes dangerous.6 Purify plant water before drinking it.

concepts.title: Myth check: the solar still
concepts.contentHtml:
In films and survival classes, the hero digs a pit, stretches a plastic sheet over it and drinks the desert. It is clever: the still draws moisture from the ground and from any plants you add, the water condenses on the plastic and drains into a cup under the lowest point.

Myth A solar still will keep you alive in the desert.
Reality The numbers are against it. The Army's manual says a still takes about 24 hours to give 0.5 to 1 litre of water,1 and that you need at least three stills to meet one person's daily needs. Each one means digging a bowl-shaped hole about a metre across and 60 centimetres deep2 in a spot that gets sun most of the day, and every spadeful costs sweat. The plastic must not touch the sides of the hole, or the earth soaks the water back up.3 Against a desert need that can reach 19 litres a day, a still is a supplement, never a plan.
Myth Follow any animal and it will lead you to water.
Reality Only some will. Grazers and grain-eating birds stay close to water; meat-eaters, birds of prey and long-flying water birds do not.

Wait, really? A still's best trick is not making water but cleaning it. Pour salty or polluted water into a trench dug about 25 centimetres outside the still's lip, and the soil filters it as the still draws it in; the manual says this works extremely well when salt water is your only source.4 And of the Army's three designs, the humble vegetation bag gives the best yield.5

title: Why Clear Water Can Kill
description: Invisible germs, how they reach a stream, and John Snow's pump in Broad Street
tryIt: On your next camping trip, sketch the site: mark your water point upstream of the tents and a toilet spot at least 60 metres from the water and downstream.

concepts.title: How it works: germs you cannot see
concepts.contentHtml:
Day three, and there it is: a stream so clear you can count the pebbles. Every instinct says drink. The trouble is that the things in water that kill people are far too small to see, and the clearest water can carry them.

The World Health Organization estimates that water contaminated with germs causes about 505,000 deaths from diarrhoea every year,1 and spreads cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio. The source is nearly always faeces. In 2022, at least 1.7 billion people drank from a source contaminated with faeces.2

The doctor who proved that water carries this kind of disease was a Londoner, John Snow. In 1854 cholera exploded around Broad Street in Soho: within 250 yards of one street corner there were more than 500 fatal attacks in ten days.3 Most experts blamed miasma, bad air.4 Snow suspected the much-used street pump, but when he examined its water on the evening of 3 September he found so little impurity that he hesitated.5 So he turned detective. He copied the cholera deaths from the General Register Office, went house to house, and found that nearly all the deaths had taken place within a short distance of the pump.

The exceptions clinched it. The workhouse in Poland Street had its own well, and of 535 inmates only five died of cholera.6 A brewery near the pump had more than seventy workmen and none fell seriously ill:7 they drank malt liquor. A widow in Hampstead, who had not been near Broad Street for months, had a large bottle of its water carted to her every day because she preferred it,8 and died of cholera. On 7 September Snow put his evidence to the parish Board of Guardians, and on 8 September the pump's handle was removed.9 The germ itself, Vibrio cholerae, was not isolated until 1883.10

concepts.title: In the field: choosing and guarding a source
concepts.contentHtml:
You cannot see germs, so you manage the odds: pick the cleanest source you can, keep your own waste away from it, and then treat it anyway.

  1. Rank your sources. Rain caught in clean containers is the best bet. Running water beats still water, and stagnant, polluted water in the tropics often carries blood flukes.
  2. Look upstream. Water near human settlements needs treating most of all; farm run-off where cattle graze and sewage from villages upstream count as contamination too.1
  3. Collect above camp. Draw drinking water upstream of your camp,2 and never foul the ground around it.
  4. Dig a cat hole. Bury your poop at least 20 centimetres (8 inches) deep and at least 60 metres (200 feet) from lakes and streams,3 downstream from where anyone collects water.
  5. Wash your hands before handling food and after the toilet; if there is no soap and water, use a hand sanitiser with at least 60% alcohol.
  6. Walk away from chemical water. Water containing fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting it.4 Find another source.
Safety Diarrhoea, vomiting and stomach pain are the usual signs of bad water. Children, pregnant women, people over 65 and anyone with a weakened immune system are at higher risk. Keep drinking to replace lost fluid and get medical help as soon as you can: Giardia, for example, is treated with prescription medicine.5

concepts.title: Myth check: clear, cold and running
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A clear, fast mountain stream is safe to drink.
Reality Water carrying bacteria, viruses and parasites sometimes looks clean, and the CDC says drinking straight from a clear mountain stream is generally not safe.1 Giardia, a gut parasite spread in faeces, shows why: it can survive for weeks to months outside the body,2 and swallowing just a few is enough to make you ill.3

Worse, the evidence hides. Giardia symptoms usually start 1 to 2 weeks after infection and last 2 to 6 weeks,4 so the hiker who says "I drank from that stream and I was fine" may simply have been home before the cramps began. In the United States alone, more than a million people a year get sick from it.5

Myth Removing the pump handle stopped the Broad Street epidemic.
Reality It is the most famous moment in public health, but Snow himself was careful. He wrote that the number of attacks had already fallen before the handle came off,6 perhaps because most residents had fled, and that he could not say whether it had fallen faster than that explained. The CDC's anniversary account says the removal prevented more deaths;7 Michigan State University's John Snow project notes the epidemic was already subsiding.8 What nobody doubts now is that the water carried the disease.

Wait, really? Snow's strongest proof came from south London, where the pipes of two water companies ran down the same streets.9 One group of customers got water containing London's sewage, the other water free of it. In the houses supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company, deaths were between eight and nine times as many as in those supplied by the Lambeth Company.10

title: Making It Safe
description: Boiling and altitude, what filters catch and miss, chemical drops and sunlight in a bottle
tryIt: Fill a clean, clear plastic bottle with tap water, lay it on its side on a dark surface in full sun for six hours and feel how warm it gets: the same set-up, with clear water, is how solar disinfection works.

concepts.title: How it works: heat, holes and chemistry
concepts.contentHtml:
You have a fire, a battered pot and a pool of tea-coloured water. Time for the oldest water technology there is. Ancient Sanskrit and Greek writings already recommended filtering through charcoal, exposing water to sunlight, boiling and straining,1 though it took thousands of years for people to realise that their senses alone were not accurate judges of water quality.2

Heat is the surest weapon. Gut germs die faster the hotter the water: even 60 °C works if you hold it there for 30 minutes,3 the principle behind pasteurisation. The CDC's travel guide says every organism that can make you ill from drinking water is killed within seconds at boiling point.4 Boiling is not strictly necessary, but it is the only easy sign of "hot enough" that needs no thermometer. Altitude lowers the boiling point, by roughly 0.5 °C for every 150 metres you climb,5 yet even at about 4,900 metres water still boils at around 83 °C,6 well above what gut germs survive.

Filters work by size, and the sizes vary enormously. A Giardia cyst is about 8 by 19 micrometres, a Cryptosporidium oocyst 4 to 6, a gut bacterium about half a micrometre across and a virus a mere 0.03. So a filter with pores of 1 micron stops the parasites, one of 0.3 micron stops bacteria too, and neither stops viruses.7 Chemicals such as chlorine bleach and iodine do the opposite job: they kill bacteria and viruses but work poorly on parasites.8 That is why the CDC's next best method after boiling is to filter and then disinfect.

concepts.title: In the field: four ways to make it safe
concepts.contentHtml:
Pick the method that suits your kit, but the order of play is always the same: clear the water first, then kill what is in it. And if all else fails, there is sunlight in a bottle.

  1. Clear it. Let muddy water stand (the Army allows 12 hours) or strain it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter, then draw off the clear water.
  2. Boil it. Bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 6,500 feet1 (about 2,000 metres). Let it cool and store it covered. Short of fuel? Heat it to the first small bubbles, take it off the heat and keep it covered for 30 minutes.2
  3. Dose it. With unscented household bleach of 5–9% sodium hypochlorite, add 2 drops per litre, double that for cloudy or very cold water,3 stir and wait at least 30 minutes. The Army's iodine dose is 5 drops of 2% tincture in a canteen of clear water, 10 if it is cloudy or cold, then a 30-minute wait.
  4. Filter, then disinfect. Most pump filters remove parasites; add a chemical afterwards to deal with bacteria and viruses.
  5. Or use the sun. Fill clean, clear plastic bottles with clear water and lay them on their sides in full sun for 6 hours, or for 2 days if it is cloudy.4
  6. Rinse the threads. After treating a bottle, loosen the cap and tip it so treated water washes the threads your mouth touches.5
Safety Let boiled water cool before you handle it, and use only unscented bleach. Avoid iodine-treated water if you are pregnant, have thyroid problems or are sensitive to iodine, and nobody should drink it for more than a few weeks at a time.6 None of these methods removes fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material.

concepts.title: Myth check: ten-minute boils and charcoal filters
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth To be safe you must boil water for ten minutes.
Reality The agencies disagree with each other, but none asks for ten. The Army's 1992 manual said to boil for 1 minute at sea level plus 1 minute for every extra 300 metres, or simply 10 minutes anywhere. The CDC says 1 minute, or 3 above 6,500 feet; Health Canada says 2 minutes above 2,000 metres;1 and the WHO says a rolling boil is enough on its own, with no extra time for altitude. A 2025 review by CDC scientists found that, in models, every listed pathogen was knocked down in 1 minute or less at boiling point, from sea level to 10,000 feet.2 The extra minute is a safety margin for people who misjudge when water is boiling,3 and it costs fuel.
Myth A layered sand and charcoal filter makes water safe to drink.
Reality It makes water look and smell better. The Army is explicit that filters of cloth, sand, crushed rock and charcoal only clear the water and make it more palatable:4 you still have to purify it. Charcoal removes odour and soaks up some chemicals, and activated charcoal traps germs but does not kill them.5

Wait, really? John Snow spotted this in London. Water for Millbank Prison, taken from the Thames, was filtered through sand and charcoal until it looked as clear as the Chelsea Company's supply, yet in every epidemic its inmates suffered far more from cholera than the people in the neighbouring streets.6

title: Storing Water and Deadly Myths
description: Keeping water safe once you have it, and what seawater, urine, cactus and snow really do
tryIt: Set up a three-day water store at home: wash and sanitise a food-grade container, fill it, label it with the date, and set a reminder to replace the water in six months.

concepts.title: How it works: why salt water makes you thirstier
concepts.contentHtml:
Day five, and you have reached the coast. The sea runs to the horizon and you are in the position of Coleridge's Ancient Mariner: "Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink.1" He was right, and the reason is your kidneys.

Seawater is about 4 percent salt,2 the Army reckons. Your cells need some salt, but your kidneys can only make urine that is less salty than seawater.3 So to get rid of the salt in a drink of seawater you have to pass more water than you drank: the Army puts the cost at about 2 litres of body fluid to clear the waste from 1 litre of seawater. As NOAA puts it, eventually you die of dehydration even as you become thirstier.4

The other famous substitutes fail for related reasons. Urine contains harmful body wastes and is about 2 percent salt:5 drinking it hands your kidneys back the job they have just done. Blood is salty, is digested like food so needs extra water, and may carry disease. Alcohol dehydrates you and clouds your judgement. The Army's sea-survival list is blunt: do not drink seawater, do not drink urine, do not drink alcohol.6

Salt can be beaten, but only with kit. Reverse osmosis filters remove salt as well as germs,7 and the hand-pumped desalinators carried in life rafts can make 6 to 35 gallons of drinking water a day if pumped continuously.8 A little seawater splashed into your rainwater, the Army adds, will hardly be noticeable.

concepts.title: In the field: storing and carrying
concepts.contentHtml:
Once you have safe water, the job is keeping it safe, and having enough stored before the next emergency arrives. The CDC's advice for a home store is precise.

  1. Work out how much. At least 1 gallon (about 3.8 litres) per person per day, for at least 3 days; try for a 2-week supply.1 Store extra for pregnant women, people who are ill, pets and hot climates.2
  2. Choose the container. Best is a food-grade water container. Otherwise pick one with a tight-closing top, made of something durable and unbreakable (not glass), ideally with a narrow neck. Never reuse one that held bleach, pesticides or other toxic chemicals.3
  3. Sanitise it. Wash it with soap and rinse, then shake it with 1 teaspoon of unscented bleach in 1 quart (about a litre) of water so the solution touches every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, pour it out and let it air-dry before filling it with clean water and closing the lid tightly.
  4. Label and date it. Mark it "drinking water" with the date, and replace the water every six months.4
  5. Store it cool and dark, at 10–21 °C (50–70 °F), out of direct sunlight5 and away from petrol and pesticides.
  6. Keep hands out. Pour it, or use a clean scoop each time; never dip your hands in.
  7. On the move, carry it inside you. In the desert the Army says to drink half a litre an hour below 38 °C and a litre an hour above it,6 rather than saving the bottle.
Safety Never drink water from radiators or boilers that are part of a home heating system.7 Keep stored water well away from fuel and garden chemicals. If you drive into hot, remote country, carry extra food and water in case you are stranded,8 and tell someone where you are going and when you will be back.

concepts.title: Myth check: cactus juice and mouthfuls of snow
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Cut open a cactus and you will find a reservoir of fresh water.
Reality The National Park Service at Saguaro National Park calls the classic film scene, a thirsty Westerner hacking open a barrel cactus for handfuls of clear, cold water, Hollywood fantasy:1 cactus juices are so rich in organic acids that the water stored inside is not fit to drink.2 The sources do not quite agree. An older Park Service handbook allows that the thick, bitter juice squeezed from a barrel cactus might, in extreme conditions, prevent death from thirst,3 and the Army's manual still describes mashing the pulp and sucking out the juice, while warning that cutting into one without a machete is slow, spiny work.4 Treat it as a desperate last resort, never a plan.
Myth In snow country, just eat snow.
Reality Eating snow or ice chills you and leads to more dehydration,5 and trying to melt it in your mouth can cause internal cold injuries. Melt it completely first, in a container near the fire, starting with a little and adding more as it turns to water. Then purify it: snow is no purer than the water it came from.6

Wait, really? Given the choice, melt ice rather than snow: a cup of ice gives more water than a cup of snow and melts faster. Even the frozen sea can help. In time sea ice loses its salt, and the old ice is the bluish kind with rounded corners; new ice, grey and milky, is still salty.
